facts.statement: Born Charleston 17 April 1806, died there 11 June 1870; raised by his maternal grandmother; law, journalism and professional authorship.
Mississippi journeys supplied literary material; New York friendships supported his career while his home remained in South Carolina.
Martin Faber (1833), Guy Rivers (1834), The Yemassee and The Partisan (1835); historical romances cover colonial Carolina and the Revolution.
Woodlands became his home in 1836; library wing added in 1859; the house burned in 1862 and again in 1865, destroying much of his library.
Defended slavery and supported the Confederacy; later scholarly recovery includes letters and the 2011 digital Simms edition.

uncertainties.statement: Sources disagree on the year of admission to the bar (1826/1827); the page gives no year. No military service, rank or order is asserted; none is established by the sources used here.

en.tagline: Carolina’s forests, frontier wars and historical romance.
en.intro: A Charleston writer made the Carolina forest a world of war, divided loyalties and family tragedy. In The Yemassee, the threatened colony and the household of Sanutee meet inside the same historical storm.
en.orientation: Simms wrote from South Carolina while maintaining literary friendships in New York. His regional commitments developed into a defence of slavery and support for the Confederacy; the war then shattered the society in which he had worked.
origin: Born in Charleston on April 17, 1806, Simms grew up with his maternal grandmother after his mother’s death and his father’s departure west. Her Revolutionary stories joined the books he read. He studied law and entered journalism, but writing became his profession.

Journeys to Mississippi in the 1820s and 1831 carried him through a frontier still undergoing settlement. Rivers, roads, encounters and remembered stories supplied material long after those journeys ended.
career: New York offered publishers and lasting friendships, not a permanent departure from Carolina. Martin Faber appeared in 1833, Guy Rivers in 1834, and The Yemassee and The Partisan in 1835. Fiction joined poetry, editing, history and biography in his working life.

From 1836, Woodlands on the Edisto River was his home. He enlarged it with a library wing in 1859. Fire struck in 1862; the house burned again in 1865, with much of his library. Rebuilding followed, but the loss reached into the materials of his profession. He died in Charleston on June 11, 1870.
literature: The Yemassee sets its colonial conflict in 1715; The Partisan begins a cycle of Revolutionary romances. Across these books, historical events become the pressure under which allegiance, courage and family obligations are tested.
en.legacy: His reputation outlived him unevenly. The publication of his letters and renewed editions brought readers back; the South Caroliniana Library’s digital edition, launched in 2011, opened his separately published works to a wider public.
en.bridge: Begin with The Yemassee: the Carolina landscape, the approaching war and Sanutee’s divided household concentrate the larger ambitions of Simms’s historical fiction.
